newsitem.title: BELGIUM: New EU treaty gives EU parliament more powers.
newsitem.headline: New EU treaty gives EU parliament more powers.

text.p: The new European Union treaty clinched on Wednesday gives the European Parliament more decision-making power over jobs, social and health issues but weakens its influence over funds for the EU's poorer states.

From now on, EU governments will have to win the approval of the directly elected EU assembly before they can turn into law proposals on jobs, equal opportunities, public health, openness, fighting fraud, customs cooperation and data protection.
The decision by EU leaders at their summit in Amsterdam increases the number of policy areas where Euro-deputies have the so-called right of co-decision.
The list already includes policy on the internal market, transport, environment and development.

But the summit bowed to pressure from the Union's four poorest states -- Spain, Portugal, Greece and Ireland -- to limit Euro-MPs' powers over the funds the EU grants to these countries to help them catch up with their richer neighbours.

The new treaty, thrashed out after more than a year of negotiation between the EU's 15 governments, fell far short of parliament's original demands, in particular by postponing changes to the balance of power in the EU bloc until new members from central and eastern Europe join early next century.

Parliament President Jose-Maria Gil-Robles said the summit's meagre results showed that the system of government-to- government negotiations, where each fought for "its individual and electoral interests", was well past its sell-by date.
The overall interests of EU citizens could only be defended when the assembly had a real say in such talks, Gil-Robles said.

The new EU treaty did answer some of the parliament's other long-standing requests, such as allowing it more say over its own internal affairs, which have until now been decided by the EU's Council of Ministers.

It gives the assembly the right to change its statutes so that Euro-MPs from all countries in the 15-member bloc are paid the same wage, a reform which parliament officials say would help stamp out cases of deputies fiddling their expenses.
